name: Alfred Powerpack
tagline: Build a local launcher with search, snippets, clipboard history, and workflows

pricing.notes: Sold as a one-time licence; canonical monthly amount is null.

tiers.name: Single Licence
tiers.limits: 1 user on up to 2 Macs; includes Alfred 5 Powerpack features and Alfred 5 updates.
tiers.notes: One-time £34, converted to $45.87 at ECB reference rates on 2026-08-13; future major versions are not included.

tiers.name: Mega Supporter
tiers.limits: 1 user on all personally owned Macs; lifetime upgrades to future Alfred versions.
tiers.notes: One-time £59, converted to $79.60 at ECB reference rates on 2026-08-13.

tiers.name: Corporate
tiers.limits: Multiple activations; public numeric price and activation counts are not stated.

pricing.freeTierCaps: No free Powerpack tier; the Alfred core app is free and has no published numeric usage cap.
pricing.billingTerms: one-time licences; no monthly or annual plan
pricing.hiddenCosts: The cheaper Single Licence covers only 2 Macs and excludes future major-version upgrades; Mega Supporter is required for all personal Macs and lifetime upgrades.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For Alfred Powerpack, build a local launcher with search, snippets, clipboard history, and workflows. The hard boundary is years of macos integration, workflow ecosystem, reliability, and community, plus os integration polish and maintenance.
coreLoopDIY: Build a local launcher with search, snippets, clipboard history, and workflows, expose keyboard-first controls, and store settings locally.
requirements: only the permissions required by the selected feature
whatYouLose: years of macOS integration, workflow ecosystem, reliability, and community
commercial support and rapid compatibility fixes
ongoingBurden: permissions, accessibility APIs, sandboxing, signing, notarization, OS regressions, updates, backups, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Alfred Powerpack because small utilities are technically reproducible, but customers pay for polish and immediate fixes when an OS update breaks a daily habit. The recurring cost buys permissions, accessibility APIs, sandboxing, signing, notarization, OS regressions, updates, backups, and support, not just the visible interface.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Powerpack Single User plan and a single-purpose local Mac app DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Alfred Powerpack in an empty repository.
Use Swift 6, SwiftUI, AppKit where necessary, SQLite, and the macOS Keychain; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: build a local launcher with search, snippets, clipboard history, and workflows, expose keyboard-first controls, and store settings locally.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create a menu-bar app with a searchable command window and global hotkey.
Implement only the primary feature and one settings screen instead of a plugin platform.
Request permissions just in time and explain why each is needed before opening System Settings.
Store configuration locally, support export or import, and never capture unrelated user content.
Add launch-at-login, update-check opt-in, diagnostics export, and a complete uninstall note.
Write unit tests for transformation logic and one UI test for the core keyboard workflow.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out a third-party extension marketplace.
Deliberately leave out cloud accounts and cross-device sync.
Deliberately leave out broad automation that executes untrusted scripts.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
